A stale copy can never stop a run, so the milestone's tasks and every later run reach the tests with no refresh step for anyone to remember. Every run silently overwrites the user's real plugin installation, including one deliberately pinned to a released version. The byte-identity check becomes empty, since it only compares the suite's own fresh copy with its source, so the suite stops testing what a user actually has installed.

The suite stops driving the user's standing installation. For each run it installs the built tree into a throwaway location under pytest's temporary directory and points the host CLI at it, for example claude --plugin-dir for Claude Code, a temporary CODEX_HOME for Codex, and a temporary home for Antigravity's fixed ~/.gemini path. The user's installed copies are never read or written, so no copy can be stale. Staleness is gone by construction, and the user's real installation is never touched, so the suite is both always fresh and fully non-invasive. It goes against the goal's wording that the suite drives each host's installed plugin copy, and it gives up checking that the documented install yields a working plugin. A temporary home or CODEX_HOME may also lose the CLI's login and settings, which today the run takes from the user's real HOME. Whether it fits depends on the axes the installed-copy-location and freshness-check questions own.

The milestone states nothing about refreshing. Bringing the installed copies up to date counts as environment setup the maintainer does outside the milestone's work, before the tasks that run the suite. No remedy text is added for Claude Code or Codex, and the suite, its stop line, and CONTRIBUTING.md say nothing more about it than they do today. It adds nothing to the milestone or the repository. Refreshing a local install is a one-off fact about one machine, not a deliverable. A task that runs the suite on Codex or Antigravity stops on the prerequisite line with no remedy written for Codex. The milestone's pass on all three hosts then depends on an unrecorded manual step, which the next maintainer or contributor has to rediscover.

open-question.question: Does this milestone update the dated hands-on blocks heading scripts/hosts/claude/settings.toml and scripts/hosts/codex/settings.toml once the suite passes on those hosts? Each block is the one record of a host's hands-on check, naming the installed version and the points the run covered. Antigravity's cites the suite for its 2026-10-26 re-check; Claude Code's (2026-10-18, claude 2.1.302, its dispatch points carried forward unchecked from 2026-10-13) and Codex's (2026-10-13, under the workspace-write sandbox) record manual runs only.
open-question.recommendation: A suite pass at a newer installed version is a re-check, which the convention has each host's one block record, and an appended sentence is the form Antigravity's block already uses for one; covering all three leaves no block citing a suite name this milestone retires and keeps the points only the manual runs covered standing on their own dates, where a whole rewrite would mark them unchecked.
open-question.alternative: Yes, for all three hosts. Each host's block keeps its text and gets one appended re-check sentence naming the date, the installed CLI version, that the check ran by the host-generic suite and under which invocation, and the points it covered, the rest standing as checked on their earlier dates; for Antigravity this sentence takes the place of the 2026-10-26 sentence's mention of the agy suite as the latest re-check, or is added after it. All three blocks end the milestone citing the same suite at the same date against the versions actually installed, so no block names a suite that no longer exists under that name and the three hosts' records read alike, which is the parity the milestone's goal is about. It touches Antigravity's block although the question's premise is that only the other two lack a suite-backed record, adding an edit whose only content is a newer date and version; it still layers dates onto blocks that already carry several, and a host on which the suite fails, depending on how the integration-defects question settles, gets no sentence, leaving the three uneven after all.

Yes, for Claude Code and Codex only. Once the suite passes on a host, that host's existing block keeps its text and gets one appended re-check sentence in the form Antigravity's 2026-10-26 sentence uses: the date, the installed CLI version (`claude` and `codex-cli` as checked), that the check ran by the on-demand suite, under which invocation (Codex's approval and sandbox mode included), and the points it covered (plugin-root resolution and both agents' dispatch), with every other point standing as checked on its earlier date. Antigravity's block is left as it is. It follows the one precedent the repository already has for a suite-backed re-check, so the edit is small, the points the earlier manual runs covered and the suite does not (Claude Code's answer-sweep run, Codex's wait and follow-up behaviour) stay recorded as checked on their own dates, and the two blocks stop being the only hosts whose dispatch record rests on manual runs alone. Each block grows another dated layer, and Claude Code's already reads as a 2026-10-18 check carrying 2026-10-13 points forward unchecked, so a reader has three dates to reconcile; Antigravity's block keeps citing the agy-only suite at `agy` 1.4.7 although the suite it names is replaced by this milestone and runs against 1.4.11. Where the suite does not pass on a host, which turns on how the integration-defects question settles, that host gets no sentence, and Codex's sentence records whichever sandbox mode the sandbox question settles on, which may differ from the workspace-write mode its block was checked under.

Yes, for Claude Code and Codex, by rewriting each block whole in the form Claude Code's 2026-10-18 block takes: a new dated block naming the installed CLI version, the suite and its invocation (Codex's sandbox mode included), and each point the suite run covered as checked, with every point of the block it replaces that the suite did not cover carried forward and marked unchecked. Antigravity's block is left as it is. Each block again reads as one check at one date against one version, which is the shape the convention describes ("the dated block ... which a later re-check updates"), and Claude Code's block stops resting its dispatch points on a carried-forward 2026-10-13 run, the very gap the question names. A rewrite is a larger edit that must restate every earlier point in carried-forward form without losing any, and marking manually observed behaviour the suite does not exercise as unchecked makes those records read weaker than they did; Antigravity's block still names the agy-only suite. It depends, like any update, on the suite passing on each host, which turns on how the integration-defects question settles.

Yes, for all three hosts in two forms: Claude Code's and Codex's blocks are rewritten whole as new dated blocks (suite-covered points checked, the rest carried forward and marked unchecked), and Antigravity's block, which already carries a full 2026-10-18 check, gets one appended re-check sentence naming the date, `agy`'s installed version, and the host-generic suite in place of the agy suite. Every block ends the milestone current and naming the suite as it now exists, while each gets the form that suits it: the two blocks whose dispatch record is weakest are made whole single-date records, and the one that already has a recent full check is only re-dated. It is the largest edit of the set and treats the three blocks inconsistently in form, so a reader cannot infer one rule for how a suite run is recorded; it carries the rewrite's cost of restating earlier points as carried forward, and like every update it applies only to hosts on which the suite passes.

No. This milestone edits no hands-on block in any `settings.toml`; the suite passing on Claude Code and Codex is recorded only by the commits that make it pass, and the blocks stay as they stand until a later deliberate hands-on check of each host, by whatever milestone next makes one, re-records them. Antigravity's block is left too, still naming the agy suite. It keeps the milestone to the suite and its references, adds no prose to three files whose blocks are already long, and keeps the hands-on block a record of deliberate checks of slot values rather than of every automated run, since a suite pass re-sources no slot value. It goes against the convention that a re-check updates the host's one record, leaving Claude Code's block naming `claude` 2.1.302 where 2.1.319 is installed, Codex's naming a 2026-10-13 manual run under the workspace-write sandbox, and both recording manual runs only after an automated check has covered their dispatch, and Antigravity's citing a suite name this milestone retires; the record of what was checked on which version is then left to commit history no reader of the block is pointed at.

open-question.question: When a suite test fails on a host because of the plugin's integration for that host and not because of the suite, is fixing the plugin (a slot value, a host definition, or a file under core/) part of this milestone? The goal requires the three existing tests to pass against all three hosts, and no automated test has driven claude or codex before.
open-question.recommendation: It is the only option under which the goal's pass on all three hosts stays reachable as written: the marker options make a test differ by host and the left-failing ones finish with the pass unmet, each needing a goal revision and handing a marked or red suite to the release pre-flight and to the sibling milestone that expects this suite to pass on all three hosts; each fix lands as its own task while the milestone holds the context that found it.
open-question.alternative: Fixing the plugin is in scope on every surface the defect needs: a slot value or any other file of the host's definition under scripts/hosts/<host>/, a runtime file under core/ (skills, agents, shared procedures), a tool under core/tools/, or scripts/build_hosts.py. Each fix lands in this milestone as its own task, with the host trees rebuilt and committed with it, so no out-of-scope handling is needed and no test is marked or left failing. The goal's requirement that the three tests pass against all three hosts stays reachable exactly as written, and the first automated drive of claude and codex is the run most likely to surface integration defects, so they are fixed by the milestone that found them while its context is held rather than handed to a later one. The milestone's size is unbounded until the suite has run: a defect in shared runtime prose or a tool changes the rendered trees of every host, owing re-runs on the hosts already passing, the Python suite at both interpreters for a tool change, and possibly a CLAUDE.md invariant edit, so a suite milestone can grow into an integration rework, and with the milestone holding the root scope once started, no other milestone can enter tasks while it does.

Fixing the plugin is in scope only within the failing host's own definition under scripts/hosts/<host>/ (a slot value, settings.toml, or a host template), rebuilt into that host's tree. A defect that needs a change under core/, a tool, or the build script is out of scope: the affected test carries a per-host expected-failure marker in the suite naming the defect, and the fix is left to a later milestone. Host-local fixes change only the one host's rendered tree, so they cannot regress the hosts already passing, the scope stays bounded, and the suite still gives a clean run that the release pre-flight can use as its gate while a core defect waits. A per-host marker is a test that differs by host, which the goal's sentence that only the prerequisite check and the invocation differ rules out, so it needs a goal revision; the marker can outlive its defect if nothing removes it; and every failure needs a judgment of whether its fix is host-local or core before the right branch is known.

alternative.id: Host-local fixes, core defects left failing

open-question.alternative: Fixing the plugin is in scope only within the failing host's own definition under scripts/hosts/<host>/ (a slot value, settings.toml, or a host template), rebuilt into that host's tree. A defect that needs a change under core/, a tool, or the build script is out of scope and is left as it is: the test stays failing on that host with nothing in the suite marking it, the defect is recorded under the milestone's Out of Scope and in its finish summary, and the fix is left to a later milestone, started once this one is finished. The scope stays bounded to suite work and host-local wording, and the suite keeps no host-specific test logic at all, so every test stays exactly one behaviour on every host and the failure stays visible on every run until the fix lands. The milestone finishes with its goal's pass on all three hosts unmet, which needs a goal revision, and a red test on a host blocks the release pre-flight's suite check on every change to its trigger paths until the later milestone lands, so the cost of the deferred defect falls on each release in between.

Fixing the plugin is not part of this milestone on any surface: the milestone changes only the suite and the references to it. Every failure judged an integration defect gets a per-host expected-failure marker in the suite naming the defect, and every fix is left to a later milestone. The milestone stays exactly a test-suite milestone with a size known in advance, no runtime file or host tree changes under it, and the suite still runs clean enough to serve the release pre-flight while each defect it found is documented in the test that found it. Even a one-line slot fix is deferred to a separate milestone, which cannot enter tasks while this root-scoped one is started, and the per-host markers contradict the goal's sentence that only the prerequisite check and invocation differ, so it needs a goal revision; the classification of a failure as a plugin defect rather than a suite defect, judged without fixing anything, is easy to get wrong.

Fixing the plugin is not part of this milestone on any surface: the milestone changes only the suite and the references to it. A test that fails on a host for an integration defect is left failing with nothing in the suite marking it, the defect is recorded under the milestone's Out of Scope and in its finish summary, and every fix is left to a later milestone, started once this one is finished. The milestone's scope is the narrowest possible and the suite stays strictly host-generic, its failures an honest report of where the plugin's integrations stand, handed to a later milestone as found. The goal's pass on all three hosts is given up wholesale and needs a goal revision, the sibling milestone starting-state-refresh, which expects a test of this suite to pass on all three hosts, inherits a red suite, and the release pre-flight's suite check fails until every deferred defect is fixed.

open-question.question: What must the prerequisite check require of the chosen host's installed plugin copy before any test runs? For Antigravity it requires the copy to be byte-identical, file for file, to the committed built tree hosts/antigravity/. On Claude Code the plugin can be loaded directly from this checkout's hosts/claude through the directory marketplace, where that comparison holds trivially, and on Codex the copy is a snapshot of hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/ taken at install time under the version it was installed at.
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: One rule for every host, generalized from the check that already works, and the only one that catches a stale copy carrying the current version, the state the Antigravity copy is in today; the installed Codex copy matches the built plugin directory of the commit it was installed from file for file, 35 files with none added, so the full-tree rule holds on Codex with no runtime-directories carve-out.
open-question.alternative: The existing third prerequisite becomes the rule for all three hosts. The copy the chosen host actually loads must match that host's plugin directory in the committed built tree file for file, a missing or extra file included: hosts/claude/ for Claude Code, hosts/antigravity/ for Antigravity, hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/ for Codex. A mismatch stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. When Claude Code loads straight from this checkout's hosts/claude, the comparison passes trivially and is still made. One rule for every host, generalized from the check that already exists. It is the only check here that catches a stale copy carrying the current version number, which is the state found on 2026-11-09: the Antigravity copy and the Claude Code cache's 1.9.0 copy both report 1.9.0 and both differ from the built trees (both still hold shared/get-current-milestone.md and lack shared/resolve-milestone.md). Any file the host adds or rewrites at install time fails it. Nobody has checked whether codex plugin add copies hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/ verbatim. On Claude Code the check tells nothing new when the loaded copy is the checkout itself, and it means something only if the located copy is the one the CLI really loads. That depends on how the sibling question on installed copy location settles.

On Antigravity and Codex the installed copy must be byte-identical to the host's built plugin directory, missing and extra files included. On Claude Code the check compares no file contents. It requires instead that the plugin source the CLI reports for cairn@cairn is this checkout's hosts/claude, loaded through the directory marketplace, and it stops the run on any other source, a cached or published copy included, even one byte-identical to the built tree. Every failure stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. On Claude Code the check becomes one that can fail for a real reason: a load from the ~/.claude/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/ copies (the 1.9.0 one is stale) or from the published marketplace. A file comparison that always passes is replaced. Claude Code never needs a reinstall after a core/ change, because the checkout is what loads. Running the suite on Claude Code needs this checkout's directory marketplace. A contributor who installed from the published cairn-claude repository is refused even when that copy is identical. Two different kinds of check now sit behind one prerequisite line, and the Claude Code one relies on reading the plugin source from claude's own report. Whether that report is the right source depends on the sibling question on installed copy location.

On every host the comparison is limited to the plugin's four runtime directories (agents/, shared/, skills/, tools/). Within those directories the installed copy must be byte-identical to the built plugin directory, missing and extra files included. Files outside them are not compared: the manifest directory, README and other top-level files, and any metadata the host adds at install time. A mismatch stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. It still catches every stale skill, procedure, agent, or tool that the tests actually exercise, including a same-version stale copy. It also tolerates whatever a host writes beside the plugin at install time or rewrites in its manifest, which on Codex has not been checked hands-on. It is weaker than the full-tree rule that exists today: a stale or wrong manifest passes unseen, even though the host reads the manifest to load the plugin. The four-directory set becomes one more rule the suite holds, and it must be kept in step with the build's [layout] mapping if a fifth runtime directory is ever added.

On every host the check compares only the version: the version recorded in the installed copy's manifest, or the version the host's own plugin listing reports, must equal VERSION. A mismatch stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. File contents are not compared. It is the cheapest check and the most robust one. It reads one value through each host's own manifest or listing, so it does not depend on which files a host copies or adds at install time, and it catches the Codex 1.7.6 copy at once. VERSION changes only at a release, and the suite runs on unreleased changes. A stale copy at the current version passes: on 2026-11-09 the Antigravity copy and the Claude Code cache's 1.9.0 copy both report 1.9.0 and both differ from the built trees. The suite would then certify old text as working, and it would lose the protection the current Antigravity check gives.

On every host the installed copy is compared byte for byte, file for file, with the host's built plugin directory, as in the full-tree rule. A mismatch prints one line naming the first differing file, and the tests then run anyway against the installed copy. Only a missing CLI or a missing copy still stops the run. The suite can be run on purpose against a copy other than the built tree, such as a published release being checked after the fact or a hand-patched copy under investigation. The run still says plainly that the copy differs. It breaks the suite's convention that a prerequisite stops the run before any test and is never a skip. A pass against a stale copy then means as much as a pass against a fresh one to anything that reads only the outcome, including the release pre-flight's check g, which runs the suite and reads its result.

No host's installed copy is compared against anything. The prerequisite check keeps only that the host's CLI resolves on PATH and that an installed copy is present, and it drops the existing Antigravity byte comparison. Tests run against whatever copy is installed. It needs no per-host comparison logic and no knowledge of what each host's install leaves on disk. It never blocks a run over a difference in a file the tests do not touch. The suite exists to check the committed integration before it is committed or released. Without a freshness check it can pass on a copy that does not contain the change under test, or fail for reasons already fixed, and nothing reports which happened. It also removes a guard that already works for Antigravity.

open-question.question: Which of the assertions that read the host's own tool-call records do the tests keep on all three hosts? Today the plugin-root test reads Antigravity's stream-json records to assert that no agent was dispatched, that a file read under the installed root's shared/ directory completed, and that a shell call running task_list.py insert under that root completed; each dispatch test reads them to assert exactly one dispatch of the named agent with the given prompt and no write or shell tool used by the dispatching process. Claude Code (--output-format stream-json) and Codex (codex exec --json) emit records of other shapes that the repository holds no parser for, and every other assertion of the three tests reads only files and git state.
open-question.recommendation: The record assertions are what make each test prove its own claim: without the read and insert records the plugin-root test shows only that something wrote the task list, and without the no-own-work assertion a dispatching process that did the task itself after its agent failed would pass, the failure the dispatch tests exist to catch; each assertion stays one behaviour on every host, and only the reading of a host's records differs, beside its invocation.
open-question.alternative: Every record assertion except the tilde pin, which a sibling question owns, is kept on all three hosts: the closing success record, no dispatch and a completed read under the installed root's shared/ directory and a completed task_list.py insert call under the root with its expected output in the plugin-root test, and exactly one dispatch of the named agent with the given prompt and no write or shell tool of the dispatching process's own in each dispatch test. Each host's records are read by a parser for that host's shape, new ones written for Claude Code's stream-json and Codex's JSONL events, each with that host's own read, shell, dispatch, and write tool names and its way of telling a completed call from a failed one. Each test keeps its full strength on every host: the plugin-root test still proves the orchestrator itself reached the shared procedures and ran the tool at the installed root, and the dispatch tests still prove the landed files are the dispatched agent's work, not the dispatching process's. Two parsers have to be written for record shapes the repository has never described, found by hands-on runs and free to change with each CLI release. The two absence assertions pass silently if a host's tool-name list is incomplete. Codex reads files through its shell rather than a file-reading tool, so "a completed read under shared/" becomes a shell command matched by its text. Where a host interleaves a dispatched agent's calls with the process's own in one stream, the parser must tell them apart. On Codex, "the named agent" can only be matched by the agent-file line opening a generic spawn's prompt, which depends on the dispatch-vehicle sibling question.

On all three hosts the tests keep only the record assertions that must find a matching record: the completed read under shared/ and the completed task_list.py insert call under the root in the plugin-root test, and the one dispatch of the named agent with the given prompt in each dispatch test. Both absence assertions are dropped (no dispatch in the plugin-root test, no write or shell tool of the dispatching process's own in the dispatch tests). Each host's records are still read by a per-host parser. A kept assertion fails loudly whenever a parser or a tool name is wrong, because it has to find its record. Nothing depends on a complete list of every host's dispatch and work tools, which is the part of a new record format most likely to be missed. The tests no longer rule out a dispatching process doing the work itself beside a dispatch, or a dispatched agent's reads and commands standing in for the orchestrator's, so a landed file or a matched read stops proving whose work it was. The two new parsers are still needed, along with the Codex read-through-shell and generic-spawn matching.

The plugin-root test keeps its record assertions on all three hosts (no dispatch, the completed read under shared/, the completed insert call under the root), read through a per-host parser for read, shell, and dispatch calls. The dispatch tests drop their record reads entirely and assert only on the landed files and git state. Records are kept exactly where no file can stand in for them: nothing on disk shows where the orchestrator read its shared procedure or which tool path it ran. The dispatch tests, whose claim the landed files already carry, need no dispatch-record parsing, and dispatch records are where the three hosts differ most (a bare name, a namespaced name, a generic spawn). The dispatch tests can no longer show that the named agent was dispatched at all, rather than a generic subagent or none, or that the dispatching process did none of the work itself. A headless process that did the task directly would pass. Read and shell parsers are still needed for two record formats, including Codex's shell-based reads.

Each dispatch test keeps its record assertions on all three hosts (exactly one dispatch of the named agent with the given prompt, and no write or shell tool of the dispatching process's own), read through a per-host parser for dispatch calls and the names of the write and shell tools. The plugin-root test drops its record reads and asserts only on the repository: the exit status and the seeded task list gaining its second section. Only the dispatch call and tool names have to be parsed, not read paths, command lines, command outputs, or call states. That is the smallest per-host parser that still keeps the dispatch tests' provenance guarantee. The plugin-root test stops testing plugin-root resolution. A gained section shows that something wrote the list, not that the orchestrator read a shared procedure or ran the tool at the installed root. A runner that wrote the section by hand, or ran a tool from another copy, would pass.

No host's records are parsed. On all three hosts the tests keep only positive claims, checked as text searches over the process's raw printed output: the installed root's shared/ path appears, a command line running task_list.py insert under the root appears, and the agent's name and the given prompt appear. Call states, command outputs, and both absence assertions are dropped. One host-neutral assertion form serves every host and no parser or tool-name list is written, so only the invocation differs per host, as the goal states, and a CLI changing its record shape breaks nothing. A search passes on a mere mention. A path quoted in skill text or a tool result, a failed read, a dispatched agent's call, or the dispatch prompt echoed back would all satisfy it. On a host whose skill text arrives with the root already resolved, the shared/ path can appear without any read happening, so the plugin-root claims can pass vacuously.

No assertion reads a host's tool-call records on any host. The suite asks for no machine-readable output mode, and every test asserts only on the exit status, files, and git state: the plugin-root test on its seeded task list gaining a second section, and the dispatch tests on their landed files and repository state as they do today. The record assertions are removed, on Antigravity as well. Nothing host-specific is left in any assertion: no parser, tool-name list, or record shape is written or maintained for any host, and the three tests are the same code on every host with only the invocation differing. The suite gives up the claims only records carry. The plugin-root test no longer shows the installed root was resolved or used, and the dispatch tests no longer show the named agent was dispatched or that the dispatching process did no work itself. Antigravity's existing coverage of both shrinks too.

No assertion reads a host's tool-call records on any host. Instead, the plugin-root test's shell-call claim moves to a side channel the suite controls: a python3 shim placed first on the PATH the headless process inherits, which appends its arguments to a log under pytest's temporary directory and then runs the real interpreter. The test asserts that the log holds a task_list.py insert run under the installed root, plus the task list's second section. The read-under-shared/ claim and the dispatch tests' record claims are dropped, and the dispatch tests assert only on files and git state. The proof that the orchestrator ran the tool at the installed root survives on every host in one host-neutral form read from a file, with no record parser, and it does not change when a CLI changes its output format. It relies on each host's shell keeping the inherited PATH and on the log location being writable from the host's shell. A shell that rebuilds PATH from the user's profile silently bypasses the shim and fails the test for a reason unrelated to the plugin, and writability depends on the Codex sandbox-mode sibling question. The shared-read and dispatch-provenance claims are lost, as in dropping records entirely.

open-question.question: Against which hosts does the release pre-flight run the suite, and on which changed paths? Today check g runs the Antigravity-only suite when git diff since the last release tag prints anything under scripts/hosts/antigravity/, core/agents/*.md, scripts/build_hosts.py, or agy_tests/, and CONTRIBUTING.md asks for a run before committing a change to the same path set, which names neither the Claude Code nor the Codex host definition. The two choices are asked together because they constrain each other: running only the hosts a change touched needs trigger paths kept per host, which one shared path set cannot give.
open-question.recommendation: A host's definition directory can change only that host's rendered tree, so running the hosts whose set changed keeps check g's meaning, a host integration changed since the last release, for all three hosts at the cost the change earns: a one-host slot edit owes one host's run, CLI, and fresh copy, from the maintainer at release and from a contributor before committing, and each set is the one shared list plus that host's own directory; the broad sets would run every host on nearly every release.
open-question.alternative: Check g keeps one trigger set per host: that host's definition directory (scripts/hosts/claude/, scripts/hosts/antigravity/, or scripts/hosts/codex/) plus the host-neutral paths core/agents/*.md, scripts/build_hosts.py, and the suite's directory. The pre-flight diffs each set against <LAST_TAG>..HEAD and runs the suite only against the hosts whose set printed anything, so a host-neutral change runs all three and a change to one host's definition runs that host alone. CONTRIBUTING.md states the same per-host sets and asks for a run against each host whose set the change touches. Run cost and the installed-CLI requirement follow what actually changed: a release that touched only the Codex definition needs only codex installed and its copy fresh, and no host is run for a change that cannot affect it. Three path lists plus a shared part are kept by hand in two files and must grow with every added host, and the pre-flight needs a run that names one host, so its viability depends on the sibling axis of how a run selects its host; core/skills/, core/shared/, and core/tools/ still trigger no run.

Check g keeps one shared trigger path set, today's widened to every host definition: all of scripts/hosts/, core/agents/*.md, scripts/build_hosts.py, and the suite's directory. When git diff --name-only <LAST_TAG>..HEAD prints anything under that set, the pre-flight runs the suite against all three hosts (Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex), and any host's failure or prerequisite stop stops the release. CONTRIBUTING.md names the same path set and asks for a run against all three hosts before committing a change to it. Keeps check g's present shape, one diff over one path list and one pass/fail, while closing the gap that a change to the Claude Code or Codex host definition owes no run; one list kept in two places stays easy to keep in step. A change to one host's slot value or settings.toml runs the full headless suite on all three hosts, each test a model-driven session bounded only by the host's own limit, and needs all three CLIs installed with up-to-date copies before that release can pass; changes to core/skills/, core/shared/, and core/tools/, which the plugin-root test exercises through submit-task, still trigger no run.

Check g keeps one shared trigger path set covering every input to a host's rendered tree and the suite: all of core/ (skills, shared, tools, agents), all of scripts/hosts/, scripts/build_hosts.py, and the suite's directory. Any change under it since the last tag runs the suite against all three hosts. CONTRIBUTING.md names the same set and asks for a run against all three hosts before committing a change to it. Every path the three tests exercise is a trigger, so a change to the submit-task skill, a shared procedure, or the task-list tool, which the plugin-root test drives, can no longer ship unrun; the set is still one short list. Nearly every release changes something under core/, so the check runs almost always, at the full three-host cost of model-driven headless sessions per release, and CONTRIBUTING.md would owe a three-host run before most commits, which a contributor without all three CLIs cannot give.

Check g keeps a broad host-neutral trigger set (all of core/, scripts/build_hosts.py, and the suite's directory), whose change runs the suite against all three hosts, and one per-host set, that host's directory under scripts/hosts/, whose change alone runs the suite against that host only. CONTRIBUTING.md states the same split. Covers every path the tests exercise, as the broad shared set does, while a release or commit that touched only one host's definition still owes a run against that host alone. Because almost every release changes core/, the per-host narrowing rarely takes effect in the pre-flight and mostly buys its benefit at commit time, at the price of keeping the per-host lists and a host-naming run, the latter depending on the sibling axis of how a run selects its host.

Check g drops its path filter: every release runs the suite against all three hosts, with no git diff step. No trigger list exists to fall out of step with what the tests exercise, matching the reasoning that keeps the CI workflow free of a paths filter, and every release is known to pass on every host it ships. Every release, a version-only patch included, pays the full three-host headless run and needs all three CLIs installed and their copies refreshed first, and the pre-flight and CONTRIBUTING.md no longer share one rule.

Check g and CONTRIBUTING.md keep today's coverage and path set, scripts/hosts/antigravity/, core/agents/*.md, scripts/build_hosts.py, and the suite's directory, running the suite against Antigravity only; they change only to follow the suite's new name and command, and Claude Code and Codex runs are left to the maintainer's discretion. The release pre-flight runs the suite on no host: check g is removed and the opening sentence's Antigravity clause with it, leaving six checks. A release is never blocked by a missing CLI, a stale installed copy, or a slow model-driven session on any host, and the suite's per-host requirements stay a development concern rather than a release gate. Nothing at release time checks that the shipped integrations still run under the installed CLIs, the one guarantee check g was added to give, and the goal names the release pre-flight among the references that follow the suite rather than ones that go away.

open-question.question: Where do the suite's per-host values live: the CLI command and its flags, the plugin directory in the built tree, the installed root, and whatever tool names and record shapes the tests read? Today they are Antigravity-bound module constants and fixtures in the suite's Python files, while everything else about a host is declared under scripts/hosts/<host>/, where adding a host needs no host-specific Python.
open-question.recommendation: The values only the suite uses stay beside the per-host record-reading code that uses them, while the plugin directory and the rendered plugin root each definition already declares are read from its settings.toml and typed nowhere a second time; the build's schema and template discovery stay untouched and no test data enters its input, and the suite runs only under the pinned interpreter, which has `tomllib`.
open-question.alternative: The values a host definition already declares, at least plugin_dir and the definition's own name and built tree, are read by the suite from scripts/hosts/<host>/settings.toml with tomllib; the values only the suite needs (the CLI command and its flags, the installed root, the tool names and parameter keys) and the per-host record-parsing code stay in the suite's Python as one per-host entry. The build and the definitions' key set are unchanged. No value is written in two places and the build still needs no change, since the suite only reads settings.toml, while the suite-only values that have no meaning to the build stay out of the build's input. A new host still needs host-specific Python in the suite for its CLI and its records, and the suite becomes a second reader of settings.toml, coupled to a format the build owns and validates for its own purposes; reading TOML ties the suite to Python 3.11 or later, which the pinned interpreter gives but the 3.9 floor run does not.

Every per-host value stays in the suite's own Python, generalised from today's Antigravity-bound constants into one per-host entry each for Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex: the CLI command and its flags, the built-tree plugin directory, the installed root, the tool names and parameter keys, and per-host code that turns each host's event records into the steps the tests read. The suite reads nothing under scripts/hosts/, the build and the host definitions are left unchanged, and the plugin directory each definition already declares as plugin_dir is written a second time in the suite. Nothing outside the on-demand suite changes: build_hosts.py, its SETTINGS_SCHEMA (which refuses any unknown settings key), and the committed hosts/ trees are untouched, and record parsing, which has to be code for at least the event-correlating shapes, sits in the same files as the values it reads. Adding a host then needs host-specific Python in the suite, breaking the rule that a host is a definition directory under scripts/hosts/ and nothing more, and the duplicated plugin directory (empty for Claude Code and Antigravity, plugins/cairn for Codex) can drift from the definition with no check catching it.

The declarative per-host values (the CLI command and its flags, the installed root or the rule for finding it, the tool names and parameter keys the assertions read) move into each host's settings.toml as one new table, added to the build's SETTINGS_SCHEMA so every definition must carry it with the same key set, and read by the suite with plugin_dir beside them. How each host's event records are parsed stays per-host code in the suite, selected by the record format the table names. Everything declarative about a host lives in its one definition and the build's existing identical-key-set validation catches a definition that forgets a suite value, so a new host's values are written once beside the rest of its declaration. The build is changed to accept and validate keys it never uses for rendering, mixing on-demand test data into the build's input, and a host whose record format is new still needs suite Python, so the no-host-specific-Python rule holds only for hosts that reuse an existing parser; how much record handling is needed at all depends on which record assertions the tests keep, an axis the host tool-call record question owns.

As the settings-table option, one new table in each host's settings.toml, added to the build's schema and read by the suite, but the table also declares each host's record shapes as data: which events are tool calls, where the tool name, its arguments, and its outcome sit, and how a call is matched to its result, all read by one generic parser in the suite with no per-host code. Adding a host needs no Python at all, in the build or the suite, which carries the definition-only rule for hosts over to the suite exactly. The three formats differ in structure, not only in names (Antigravity's step_update carries a final state per step, while Claude Code's stream-json and Codex's JSONL pair a call and its result across separate events), so the declaration needs a small mapping language and a generic parser for it, a large mechanism for three tests on an on-demand suite, carried in the build's input; it is worth building only to the extent the tests keep record assertions, which the host tool-call record question decides.

The declarative per-host values sit in a separate file of their own under each scripts/hosts/<host>/ directory, outside settings.toml, which the build does not validate; template discovery is taught to skip it as it skips slots/, so it is never rendered into hosts/<host>/. The suite reads it with plugin_dir from settings.toml, and record parsing stays per-host code in the suite. A host's suite values live with the rest of its declaration while the build's schema and validation stay exactly as they are, so test data never enters the build's input. The build still needs one change, a discovery skip, or the file renders into the shipped tree and is published to the distribution repository; no check keeps the side files' key sets identical across hosts unless the suite makes one, and a host with a new record format still needs suite Python.

As the side-file option, a separate file under each scripts/hosts/<host>/ that template discovery skips and the build does not validate, but it also declares the host's record shapes as data for one generic parser in the suite, so the suite holds no per-host code. Adding a host is a definition directory and nothing else, with the build's schema untouched and the suite's whole per-host knowledge, records included, declared beside that host's other settings. It carries both the discovery-skip change to the build and the mapping language and generic parser the structurally different record formats need, with no build validation of either file's shape; the parser's size depends on which record assertions survive, which the host tool-call record question decides.

The per-host values, record shapes declared as data included, live in one data file per host inside the suite's own directory rather than under scripts/hosts/, read by one generic suite parser; plugin_dir is read from the host's settings.toml, and neither the build nor the definitions change. The suite holds no per-host Python and the build is left wholly untouched, with no schema change and no discovery skip, and nothing a test needs can leak into a rendered or published tree. A host's declaration is split across two directories, so adding a host means a definition under scripts/hosts/ and a data file in the suite, against the rule that a host is declared in one place, and it still needs the mapping language and generic parser for the differently structured record formats, sized by which record assertions the host tool-call record question keeps.
